title: XI. There Was No Money. There Was No Robbery
paragraphs: One point in Fetyukovitch’s speech struck everyone. He flatly denied that the fatal three thousand roubles had ever existed, and so denied that anyone could have stolen them.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” he began. “Anyone who comes to this case fresh and without prejudice will notice one odd feature in it. We have a charge of robbery, and no way at all of proving that there was anything to rob. We are told that three thousand roubles were stolen. Whether those roubles ever existed, nobody knows. Think how we came to hear of the sum, and who has actually seen the notes. The only person who saw them, and who said they had been put in the envelope, was the servant Smerdyakov. Before the catastrophe he mentioned it to the prisoner and to the prisoner’s brother, Ivan Fyodorovitch. Madame Svyetlov was told of it as well. Yet not one of these three ever saw the notes. Smerdyakov alone saw them.

“So a question arises. Suppose the notes did exist and Smerdyakov did see them. When did he see them last? Perhaps his master took the notes from under his bed and put them back in his cash-box without a word to Smerdyakov. Note this too. By Smerdyakov’s account the notes lay under the mattress. The prisoner would have had to drag them out, and yet the bed was perfectly smooth. The protocol records this with care. How could the prisoner find the notes without disturbing the bed? And how could his bloodstained hands have avoided marking the fine, spotless linen that had been so carefully laid on it?

“But I will be asked about the envelope on the floor. Yes, that envelope deserves a word or two. A moment ago I was somewhat surprised to hear the highly talented prosecutor say of himself (of himself, mark you) that without that envelope, without its being left on the floor, nobody in the world would have known that the envelope existed, or the notes inside it, and so nobody would have known the prisoner had stolen them. So by the prosecutor’s own admission that torn scrap of paper is the one proof on which the charge of robbery rests. ‘Otherwise no one would have known of the robbery, or perhaps even of the money.’ But does a scrap of paper lying on the floor prove that there was money in it, and that the money was stolen? It will be objected that Smerdyakov saw the money in the envelope. But when did he see it last? I ask you that. I spoke to Smerdyakov, and he told me he saw the notes two days before the catastrophe. Why then not picture old Fyodor Pavlovitch, locked up alone, waiting in hysterical impatience for the woman he adored, and passing the time by tearing open the envelope and taking out the notes? ‘What good is the envelope?’ he may have asked himself. ‘She will not believe the notes are in it. But if I show her thirty rainbow-colored notes in one roll, that will impress her, you may be sure. It will make her mouth water.’ So he rips the envelope open, takes out the money, and throws the envelope on the floor. He knows the money is his, and he has no fear of leaving evidence behind.

“Consider, gentlemen: could anything be more likely than this account and this action? Why should it be out of the question? And if something of the kind could have happened, the charge of robbery collapses. Where there was no money, no money was stolen. The envelope on the floor is supposed to show there had been money in it. Why may I not say the opposite, that the envelope lay on the floor because its owner had taken the money out?

“But I will be asked where the money went, if Fyodor Pavlovitch took it out of the envelope, since the police did not find it when they searched the house. First, part of the money was found in the cash-box. Second, he may have taken it out that morning, or the evening before, for some other use. He may have meant to give it away or send it off. He may have changed his mind and his plan altogether, and not thought it necessary to tell Smerdyakov beforehand. If such an explanation has even the barest chance of being true, how can anyone say so positively that the prisoner killed for the sake of robbery, and really carried out that robbery? That is to wander into the realm of fiction. If you claim something was stolen, you must produce the thing, or at least prove beyond doubt that it existed. But nobody ever saw these notes.

“Not long ago in Petersburg, a young man of eighteen, hardly more than a boy, who kept a small business as a costermonger, walked into a moneychanger’s shop in broad daylight with an ax. With extraordinary, typical audacity, he killed the shop’s master and took off fifteen hundred roubles. Five hours later he was arrested. Except for fifteen roubles that he had already managed to spend, the entire sum was found on him. What is more, when the shopman came back to the shop after the murder, he gave the police not only the exact amount stolen but the very notes and gold coins that made it up, and those same notes and coins were found on the criminal. The murderer then made a full and genuine confession. That, gentlemen of the jury, is what I call evidence! There I know the money, I see it, I touch it, and I cannot deny that it exists. Is it so in the present case? And yet here it is a matter of life and death.

“Yes, I will be told, but he was carousing that night and squandering money. He was shown to have had fifteen hundred roubles. Where did he get it? But look at the fact itself. Only fifteen hundred could be found, and the other half of the sum was nowhere to be discovered. That shows this money was not the same money, and had never been in any envelope. The preliminary inquiry proved, by a strict calculation of time, that the prisoner ran from those women servants straight to Perhotin’s, without going home, and that he had been nowhere else. So he was in company the whole time. He could not have divided the three thousand in half and hidden half of it in the town. This is exactly what has led the prosecutor to suppose that the money is hidden in some crevice at Mokroe. Why not in the dungeons of the castle of Udolpho, gentlemen? Is this supposition not far too fantastic and too romantic? And observe that if it breaks down, the whole charge of robbery is blown away. For then what became of the other fifteen hundred roubles? By what miracle did they vanish, when it is proved that the prisoner went nowhere else? And we are ready to ruin a man’s life with such tales!

“I will be told that he could not explain where he got the fifteen hundred he had, and that everyone knew he was penniless before that night. Who knew it, I ask you? The prisoner has given a clear and steady account of where that money came from. If you will have it so, gentlemen of the jury, nothing could be more probable than that account, or fit better with the prisoner’s temper and spirit. The prosecutor is charmed with his own romance. A man of weak will, we are told, who brought himself to take the three thousand so insultingly offered by his betrothed, could never have set half of it aside and sewn it up. Even if he had, he would have unpicked it every two days, taken out a hundred, and spent the lot within a month. You will remember that all this was put forward in a tone that allowed no reply. But what if the thing happened quite differently? What if you have been spinning a romance, and about quite a different kind of man? That is exactly it. You have invented a different man altogether!

“Perhaps I will be told that witnesses say he spent the whole three thousand from his betrothed in a single day, a month before the catastrophe, and so could not have divided it in half. But who are these witnesses? The court has already seen what their evidence is worth. Besides, a crust always looks bigger in another man’s hand. None of these witnesses counted that money. They all judged by eye. And the witness Maximov testified that the prisoner had twenty thousand in his hand. You see, gentlemen of the jury, psychology cuts both ways. Let me turn the other edge now and see what comes of it.

“A month before the catastrophe, Katerina Ivanovna entrusted the prisoner with three thousand roubles to send off by post. But is it true that they were entrusted to him in such an insulting and degrading way as we heard proclaimed just now? The young lady’s first statement on this was different, quite different. In the second statement we heard only cries of resentment and revenge, cries of hatred long kept hidden. The fact that the witness gave her first evidence incorrectly gives us the right to conclude that her second may be incorrect too. The prosecutor will not touch that story, he dares not (his own words). So be it. I will not touch it either. I will only venture to say this. A lofty, high-principled person, such as that highly respected young lady undoubtedly is, suddenly contradicts her first statement in court, with the plain motive of ruining the prisoner. Then it is clear that her evidence has been given neither fairly nor calmly. May we not assume that a woman bent on revenge has exaggerated a great deal? Yes, she may well have exaggerated, above all the insult and humiliation in her offering him the money. No, it was offered in a way that made it possible to take it. That is especially so for a man as easy-going as the prisoner, and above all because he expected soon to receive from his father the three thousand roubles he reckoned were owing to him. It was thoughtless of him. But it was just that irresponsible thoughtlessness that made him so sure his father would give him the money, that he would get it, and that he could therefore always send off the money entrusted to him and pay the debt.

“But the prosecutor refuses to allow that on the same day he could have set aside half the money and sewn it into a little bag. That is not his character, we are told. He could not have had such feelings. Yet the prosecutor himself spoke of the broad Karamazov nature. He cried out about the two extremes a Karamazov can hold in view at once. Karamazov is precisely such a two-sided nature, swinging between two extremes. Even in the grip of the wildest craving for revelry, he can pull himself up short if something strikes him from the other side. And on the other side is love, that new love which had flared up in his heart. For that love he needed money, oh, far more than he needed it for carousing with his mistress. If she were to say to him, ‘I am yours, I will not have Fyodor Pavlovitch,’ then he had to have money to take her away. That mattered more than carousing. Could a Karamazov fail to see it? That very worry was what he suffered from. What is improbable in his putting that money aside and hiding it for an emergency?

“But time went by, and Fyodor Pavlovitch did not give the prisoner the three thousand he expected. On the contrary, the prisoner heard that his father meant to use that sum to seduce the woman he, the prisoner, loved. ‘If Fyodor Pavlovitch does not give me the money,’ he thought, ‘I shall look like a thief to Katerina Ivanovna.’ Then the idea came to him of going to Katerina Ivanovna, laying before her the fifteen hundred roubles he still wore round his neck, and saying, ‘I am a scoundrel, but I am not a thief.’ So here we already have two reasons why he should guard that sum like the apple of his eye. They are why he should not unpick the little bag and spend it a hundred at a time. Why should you deny the prisoner a sense of honor? He has one. Grant that it is misplaced, grant that it often leads him astray. Still it exists, it is a passion in him, and he has proved it.

“But now the affair grows more tangled still. His torments of jealousy reach their height, and the same two questions torture his fevered brain more and more: ‘If I pay back Katerina Ivanovna, where will I find the means to go off with Grushenka?’ He behaved wildly in the course of that month. He drank and made disturbances in the taverns. Perhaps this was because he was miserable and strained past what he could bear. The two questions grew so sharp that at last they drove him to despair. He sent his younger brother to beg, for the last time, for the three thousand roubles. Without waiting for an answer, he burst in himself and ended by beating the old man before witnesses. After that he had no hope of getting the money from anyone, since his father would not give it to him after such a beating.

“That same evening he struck himself on the breast, on the upper part of the chest where the little bag hung, and swore to his brother that he had the means of not being a scoundrel. But he said he would still remain a scoundrel, because he foresaw he would not use that means. He did not have the character for it, he said, he did not have the willpower. Why, why does the prosecutor refuse to believe the evidence of Alexey Karamazov, given so genuinely and sincerely, so spontaneously and convincingly? And why does he, on the contrary, force me to believe in money hidden in a crevice, in the dungeons of the castle of Udolpho?

“That same evening, after the talk with his brother, the prisoner wrote that fatal letter. And that letter, we are told, is the chief proof, the most stupendous proof, that the prisoner committed robbery! ‘I shall beg from everyone, and if I do not get it I shall murder my father and take the envelope with the pink ribbon from under his mattress as soon as Ivan has gone.’ A full program of the murder, they say, so it must have been he. ‘It has all been done as he wrote,’ cries the prosecutor.

“But in the first place, this is the letter of a drunken man, written in great irritation. In the second place, what he writes about the envelope comes, once again, from what Smerdyakov told him, for he had not seen the envelope himself. And in the third place, he did write it, but how can you prove he did what it says? Did the prisoner take the envelope from under the pillow? Did he find the money? Did that money really exist? And remember, was it to get money that the prisoner ran off? He ran off in headlong haste, not to steal, but to find out where she was, the woman who had crushed him. He was not running to carry out a program, to do what he had written, that is, to commit a premeditated robbery. He ran suddenly, spontaneously, in a jealous fury. Yes! I will be told that when he got there and murdered him, he seized the money as well. But did he murder him after all? The charge of robbery I reject with indignation. A man cannot be accused of robbery if it is impossible to say exactly what he stole. That is an axiom. But did he murder him without robbing him? Did he murder him at all? Has that been proved? Is that too not a romance?”
